name: Home Intelligence

seo.title: Home Intelligence | DAVG
seo.description: A scene coordinates lighting, shades, music, and other compatible systems. The design starts with what your household wants to happen.

hero.heading: One command. Several systems. A predictable result.
hero.deck: A scene coordinates lighting, shades, music, and other compatible systems. The design starts with what your household wants to happen.

study: Halo and Halo Touch product photographs sit in the device study. A separate diagram follows interface, controller, driver and network.

chapters.title: Start with the moments you repeat.
paragraphs: You come home carrying bags. You want a lit entry, comfortable living-room light, and a clear way to stop the music left playing upstairs.
An Arrival scene sends a defined set of commands to the connected systems. A keypad can start that scene without opening an app or speaking to the house.
We begin with those repeatable moments. Then we decide what belongs in the scene, what stays independent, and who can change it.
chapters.visual: Three states of the same room: Arrival, Evening, Away. Show exactly which devices change, with a static text list alongside.

chapters.title: What actually connects the house?
paragraphs: A Control4 controller runs the project and communicates with supported equipment through its available network and control connections. Integration software tells it how each device accepts commands and reports its state.
A command sent is not always a command confirmed. A system that reports its actual state gives better feedback than one that only receives a power command.
The home network carries much of this communication. Controller selection follows the devices, rooms, connections, and processing needs of the project; it is not a ladder of prestige.
chapters.visual: Draw controller, network, lighting processor, audio, shades and interfaces as distinct roles. Mark confirmed feedback versus command-only examples.

chapters.title: Choose the control you will reach for.
paragraphs: A keypad works well for actions you know by heart. A remote keeps viewing controls in your hand; a touchscreen can show rooms, sources, and compatible intercom functions.
The app gives a broader view of the residence. It should not be the only way to turn on the lights in a guest room.
Use fewer labels and make them literal. Evening is useful only when everyone knows what it changes.
chapters.visual: Real Control4 Halo/Halo Touch, touchscreen and keypad front views beside installed-use photographs. Confirm current model and finish.

rows: Physical controls, screen preference and charging
House-wide selection and supported remote access

chapters.title: A focused room or a whole residence?
paragraphs: A room system can coordinate a television, sound, and a few lighting scenes. A residence-wide design adds shared sources, more interfaces, cross-room scenes, and a larger set of things that must work together.
Independent devices can remain independent when their existing controls suit the household. Every extra integration adds setup and an ongoing compatibility responsibility.
Write the intended behavior before selecting equipment. That makes the scope review about the house rather than a controller model number.
chapters.visual: Compare a media-room scene with the same residence expanded to entry, bedroom and outdoor zones.

chapters.title: What happens when the internet stops?
paragraphs: Some commands run within the local system. Streaming services, off-site access, and other cloud-dependent functions need their own internet or service connections.
A power outage is a different failure. The controller, network, and devices all need power; backing up one box does not keep the whole chain running.

The proposal should identify local functions, internet-dependent functions, subscriptions, and the expected behavior during each outage. Current Control4 service terms must be checked against the installed system and account.
chapters.visual: Two legible states: internet unavailable and utility power unavailable. List affected functions without a blanket “works offline” badge.

chapters.title: The last step is living with it.
paragraphs: Commissioning means testing each agreed scene from the interfaces your family will use. It also means checking room names, volume limits, access permissions, and what happens when a device is unavailable.
A takeover starts with an inventory. Existing controllers, software, wiring, account ownership, and unsupported devices can change the work before any new hardware is chosen.
At handover, the household should know how to use the everyday controls and how to request changes. Documentation keeps a future service visit from starting over.
chapters.visual: Show an example scene schedule, labeled rack and household handover sheet. Label sample documents as illustrative.

projectPaths.title: An existing home
projectPaths.body: Inventory current equipment and cable paths first. Add scenes around controls that already make sense; use available routes for interfaces and network improvements.

projectPaths.title: Rooms already opening up
projectPaths.body: Coordinate interface positions, cable routes and lighting changes before finishes close. Decide which existing devices remain in the system.

projectPaths.title: A house still on paper
projectPaths.body: Set room names, system boundaries, interface locations and rack requirements with the architect, builder and trades. Test the daily-use plan before ordering controls.

scopeOptions.label: Good — focused control
scopeOptions.scope: One defined room or group of daily scenes, compatible devices, interface setup, network review and handover.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Existing equipment must be assessed; network repairs and unsupported integrations are separate scope.

scopeOptions.label: Better — coordinated residence
scopeOptions.scope: Several rooms, shared scene logic, interface planning, documented integration behavior and commissioning across zones.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Controller capacity, wiring, third-party systems and service subscriptions follow the actual design.

scopeOptions.label: Best — comprehensive design
scopeOptions.scope: Whole-residence coordination, early trade design, detailed scene schedule, account planning and agreed support arrangements.
scopeOptions.dependencies: Scope can include more design and testing without requiring every device to join the system.

faqs.question: Can I keep my existing equipment?
faqs.answer: Often, but model numbers and control methods matter. We assess what can be integrated, what needs replacement, and what is better left on its own.

faqs.question: Does everything need a subscription?
faqs.answer: No single answer applies to every function. The proposal should list current service requirements for remote access, integrations and streaming on your specific system.

faqs.question: Can my family use it without a phone?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the design includes local interfaces for everyday actions. Keypads and remotes should cover the commands used most often.

faqs.question: What changes the project cost?
faqs.answer: Room count, interfaces, device compatibility, cable work, network condition, programming depth and takeover repairs. Support terms are a separate decision.

inquiry.heading: Start with the project you have.
inquiry.body: Tell us which rooms matter, what already exists, and when construction starts. Share plans or photographs if you have them.

openingQA.question: What should a connected home actually make easier?
answer: The actions your household repeats: arriving, watching, listening, closing the house for the night. A supported control system coordinates the required devices from a clear local interface.
The design defines what each command changes and which functions need internet service. Then the installed system is tested against that behavior.
